title: The Word becomes food fitted to each
source_text: Προσδιατρίβων δ᾿ ὁ Κέλσος οἷς οὐ νενόηκεν αἴτιος ἡμῖν γίνεται ταυτολογίας, οὐ βουλομένοις κἂν τῷ δοκεῖν ἀβασάνιστον τῶν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ λελεγμένων τι καταλελοιπέναι, φησὶν οὖν ἑξῆς ὅτι ἤτοι ὡς ἀληθῶς μεταβάλλει ὁ θεὸς, ὥσπερ οὗτοί φασιν, εἰς σῶμα θνητὸν, καὶ προείρηται ὅτι ἀδυνατεῖ· ἢ αὐτὸς μὲν οὐ μεταβάλλει, ποιεῖ δὲ τοὺς ὁρῶντας δοκεῖν καὶ πλανᾷ καὶ ψεύδεται, ἀπάτη δὲ καὶ ψεῦδος ἄλλως μὲν κακὰ, μόνως δ᾿ ἄν ὡς ἐν φαρμάκου μοίρᾳ χρῷτό τις ἤτοι πρὸς φίλους νοσοῦντας καὶ μεμηνότας, ἰώμενος, ἢ πρὸς ἐχθροὺς, κίνδυνον ἐκφυγεῖν προμηθούμενος, οὔτε δὲ νοσῶν ἢ μεμηνὼς οὐδεὶς θεῷ φίλος, οὔτε φοβεῖταί τινα ὁ θεὸς, ἵνα πλανήσας κίνδυνον διαφύγῃ, καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο λέγοιτ᾿ ἂν πῇ μὲν περὶ τῆς τοῦ θείου λόγου φύσεως, ὄντος θεοῦ, πῇ δὲ περὶ τῆς Ἰησοῦ ψυχῆς· περὶ μὲν οὖν τῆς τοῦ λόγου φύσεως ὅτι, ὥσπερ ἡ τῶν τροφῶν ποιότης πρὸς τὴν τοῦ νηπίου φύσιν εἰς γάλα μεταβάλλει ἐν τῇ τρεφούσῃ, ἢ ὑπὸ τοῦ ἰατροῦ κατασκευάζεται πρὸς τὸ τῆς ὑγείας χρειῶδες τῷ κάμνοντι, ἢ τῷ ἰσχυροτέρῳ ὡς δυνατωτέρῳ οὑτωσὶ εὐτρεπίζεται· οὕτως τὴν τοῦ πεφυκότος (τρέφειν) ἀνθρωπίνην ψυχὴν λόγου δύναμιν ὁ θεὸς τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἑκάστῳ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν μεταβάλλει, καὶ τινὶ μὲν, ὡς ὠνόμασεν ἡ γραφὴ, „λογικὸν ἄδολον γάλα“ γίνεται, τινὶ δὲ ὡς ἀσθενεστέρῳ οἱονεὶ λάχανον, τινὶ δὲ τελείῳ „στερεὰ τροφὴ“ παραδίδοται, καὶ οὐ δή που ψεύδεται τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φύσιν ὁ λόγος, ἑκάστῳ τρόφιμος γινόμενος, ὡς χωρεῖ αὐτὸν παραδέξασθαι, καὶ οὐ πλανᾷ οὐδὲ ψεύδεται. εἰ δ᾿ ἐπὶ τῆς Ἰησοῦ ψυχῆς λαμβάνει τις τὴν μεταβολὴν, αὐτῆς εἰς σῶμα ἐλθούσης, πευσόμεθα, πῶς λέγει μεταβολήν. εἰ μὲν γὰρ τῆς οὐσίας, οὐ δίδοται οὐ μόνον ἐπ᾿ ἐκείνης ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ περὶ ἄλλου λογικῆς ψυχῆς· εἰ δ᾿ ὅτι πάσχει τι ὑπὸ τοῦ σώματος ἀνακεκραμένη αὐτῷ καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ τόπου, εἰς ὃν ἐλήλυθε, καὶ τί ἄτοπον ἀπαντᾷ τῷ λόγῳ, ἀπὸ πολλῆς φιλανθρωπίας καταβιβάζοντι σωτῆρα τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων; ἐπεὶ μηδεὶς τῶν πρότερον θεραπεύειν ἐπαγγειλαμένων τοσοῦτον ἐδύνατο, ὅσον αὐτὴ ἐπεδείξατο δι᾿ ὧν πεποίηκε, καὶ ἑκουσίως εἰς τὰς ἀνθρωπίνας κῆρας ὑπὲρ τοῦ γένους ἡμῶν καταβᾶσα. ταῦτα δ᾿ ἐπιστάμενος ὁ θεῖος λόγος πολλὰ πολλαχοῦ λέγει τῶν γραφῶν. ἀρκεῖ δ᾿ ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος μίαν παραθέσθαι Παύλου λέξιν οὕτως ἔχουσαν· „τοῦτο φρονείσθω ἐν ὑμῖν, ὃ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, ὃς ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ ὑπάρχων οὐχ ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ, ἀλλ᾿ ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν,“ „καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν, γενόμενος ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου, θανάτου δὲ σταυροῦ. διὸ καὶ ὁ θεὸς αὐτὸν ὑπερύψωσε καὶ ἐχαρίσατο αὐτῷ ὄνομα τὸ ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὄνομα.“
pass_a_gloss: Dwelling further (προσδιατρίβων) on what he has not understood, Celsus becomes cause (αἴτιος) to us of repetition (ταυτολογίας), we not wishing even in appearance (κἂν τῷ δοκεῖν) to have left anything of his said things unexamined (ἀβασάνιστον). He says next: 'Either truly God changes (μεταβάλλει), as these say, into a mortal body, and it was said before that he is unable (ἀδυνατεῖ); or he himself does not change, but makes the seers seem/think (ποιεῖ δοκεῖν) and misleads (πλανᾷ) and lies (ψεύδεται). But deceit (ἀπάτη) and falsehood (ψεῦδος) are otherwise evils, but only as in the part of a drug (ἐν φαρμάκου μοίρᾳ) would one use them, either toward friends sick (νοσοῦντας) and mad (μεμηνότας), healing, or toward enemies, providing (προμηθούμενος) to escape danger (κίνδυνον). But no one sick or mad is a friend to God (θεῷ φίλος), nor does God fear (φοβεῖται) anyone so as, having misled, to escape danger.' To this it may be said partly about the nature (φύσεως) of the divine Word, being God, partly about Jesus' soul (ψυχῆς). About the nature of the Word: as the quality (ποιότης) of foods (τροφῶν) changes into milk (γάλα) in the nurse (τρεφούσῃ) to the infant's nature, or is prepared (κατασκευάζεται) by the physician for the need of health to the sick, or is readied (εὐτρεπίζεται) thus for the stronger as more able; so God changes the power (δύναμιν) of the Word, which is naturally fitted (πεφυκότος) [to nourish] the human soul, to men each according to worth (κατ᾿ ἀξίαν); and to one, as Scripture named, he becomes 'rational/word-milk unadulterated (λογικὸν ἄδολον γάλα)', to another weaker as it were vegetable (λάχανον), to another perfect (τελείῳ) 'solid food (στερεὰ τροφή)' is delivered. And the Word does not falsify his own nature, becoming nourishing (τρόφιμος) to each as he has room (χωρεῖ) to receive him; and does not mislead or lie. If someone takes the change of Jesus' soul, it having come into body, we shall inquire how he says change. If of essence (οὐσίας), it is not granted, not only for that one but not for any other rational soul (λογικῆς ψυχῆς); if that it suffers something from the body, mingled (ἀνακεκραμένη) with it, and from the place (τόπου) into which it has come, what absurd (ἄτοπον) meets the account/Word (τῷ λόγῳ) bringing down (καταβιβάζοντι) a saviour (σωτῆρα) from great philanthropy to the race of men? Since none of those formerly professing (ἐπαγγειλαμένων) to heal could do so much as it showed (ἐπεδείξατο) by what it did, even willingly (ἑκουσίως) coming down into human dooms (κῆρας) for our race. Knowing these, the divine word says many things in many places of the Scriptures; enough now to set out one saying (λέξιν) of Paul: Philippians 2:5-9.

lemmas.lemma: τοῦτο φρονείσθω ... ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο ... ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε μορφὴν δούλου λαβών ... σχήματι εὑρεθείς ... ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου ... ὑπερύψωσε ... ἐχαρίσατο ... ὄνομα τὸ ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὄνομα

pass_b_english: By lingering over things he has not understood, Celsus makes us repeat ourselves, since we do not wish even to seem to have left any of his statements unexamined. He says next: “Either God really changes, as these people say, into a mortal body, and it has already been said that he cannot; or he himself does not change, but makes those who see him think he has, and leads them astray and lies. But deceit and falsehood are evils in every other case; one might use them only as a kind of medicine, either toward friends who are sick or mad, to heal them, or toward enemies, when one is taking care to escape danger. But no one who is sick or mad is a friend of God, nor does God fear anyone, that he should lead him astray to escape danger.”

To this one may answer partly concerning the nature of the divine Word, who is God, and partly concerning the soul of Jesus. Concerning the nature of the Word: just as the quality of foods is changed into milk in the nurse to suit the nature of the infant, or is prepared by the physician to meet the sick man’s need for health, or is made ready accordingly for the stronger man, since he is more able to take it; so God changes the power of the Word, whose nature is to nourish the human soul, for each person according to his worth. To one, as Scripture has named it, he becomes “the pure milk of the word” (1 Peter 2:2); to another, who is weaker, something like vegetables (Romans 14:2); to another, who is mature, he is given as “solid food” (Hebrews 5:14). And surely the Word does not belie his own nature when he becomes nourishment for each, as each is able to receive him; he neither leads astray nor lies.

But if someone takes the change to refer to the soul of Jesus, when it came into a body, we shall ask what he means by “change”. If he means change of essence, that is not granted, either for that soul or for any other rational soul. But if he means that, being mingled with the body, it suffers something from the body and from the place into which it has come, what absurdity follows for the teaching that, out of great love for mankind, brings a Saviour down to the human race? For none of those who earlier professed to heal could do as much as this soul showed by what it did, even coming down willingly, for the sake of our race, into the ills that are the lot of men.

Knowing this, the divine word says much in many places of the Scriptures. For the present it is enough to set out one passage of Paul, which runs thus: “Have this mind among you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count being equal with God a prize to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave; and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him and granted him a name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:5-9).

choices.choice: added 'even' for κἂν τῷ δοκεῖν ('do not wish even to seem')
'it has already been said that this is impossible' -> 'that he cannot' (ἀδυνατεῖ, God as subject)
'he does not change himself' -> 'he himself does not change' (αὐτὸς μέν; the reflexive reading was wrong)
'in a different way for the stronger man, as one more able' -> 'accordingly for the stronger man, since he is more able' (οὑτωσί)
removed doubled 'for men ... for each' -> 'for each person according to his worth'
'not only in its case but not even in that of any other' -> 'either for that soul or for any other rational soul' (stiff double negative)
added 'even' for καὶ ἑκουσίως; 'brings down a Saviour' -> 'brings a Saviour down'
Philippians 2:9: 'exalted him on high' -> 'highly exalted him'; 'the name' -> 'a name' (anarthrous ὄνομα)
checked 1 Peter 2:2, Romans 14:2, Hebrews 5:14, Philippians 2:5-9 against Origen's wording

Celsus's quotation runs from 'Either God' to 'escape danger'. 'ἀδυνατεῖ' has God as subject: 'he cannot'. '(τρέφειν)' is an editorial supplement in Koetschau's text ('whose nature is to nourish'); kept. 'οὑτωσί εὐτρεπίζεται' rendered 'is made ready accordingly'. 'λογικὸν ἄδολον γάλα' (1 Peter 2:2) rendered 'the pure milk of the word' to keep Origen's play on λόγος. 'λάχανον' alludes to Romans 14:2 (ὁ ἀσθενῶν λάχανα ἐσθίει). 'στερεὰ τροφή' for the mature (τελείῳ) matches Hebrews 5:14 (also 5:12). 'τί ἄτοπον ἀπαντᾷ τῷ λόγῳ, ... καταβιβάζοντι σωτῆρα' is ambiguous: λόγος may be 'the teaching/argument' or 'the Word' bringing a Saviour down; rendered 'the teaching' since ἀπαντᾷ τῷ λόγῳ is the usual idiom for a consequence meeting an argument, but 'the Word' is possible. 'ὁ θεῖος λόγος' speaking through the Scriptures is rendered lowercase 'the divine word' (Scripture), as in 4.13. 'κῆρας' (Homeric 'dooms, fated ills') rendered 'the ills that are the lot of men'. Origen's Philippians citation omits 'ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος' (2:7b) and joins 2:7a to 2:7c-8; translated as he quotes it. 'ὄνομα τὸ ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὄνομα' has no article on ὄνομα: 'a name that is above every name'.
